paragraphs: Swamiji calls the Mahabharata the story of 'Great India': at its heart, a war between two branches of one family, the Kauravas and the Pandavas. Blind Dhritarashtra could not inherit the throne, so his younger brother Pandu ruled. When Pandu died young, Dhritarashtra raised Pandu's five sons alongside his own hundred. The goodness of the eldest Pandava, Yudhishthira, and the strength of his brothers filled Duryodhana, Dhritarashtra's eldest, with jealousy. He even had a palace of flammable materials built for them and set on fire, but the wise Vidura warned them and they escaped.

Disguised as poor Brahmin students, the brothers lived by begging. At Princess Draupadi's swayamvara, every king failed to shoot the eye of a fish by looking only at its reflection. Then Arjuna, still in disguise, strung the great bow easily and hit the mark. Home with the bride, the brothers joked to their mother Kunti that they had brought wonderful alms; she told them to share it, and since a mother's word could not be broken, Draupadi became the wife of all five.

Later Yudhishthira, a man of every virtue but fond of dice, was challenged by the crafty Shakuni using loaded dice. He lost his wealth, kingdom, brothers, himself and finally Draupadi, who was cruelly insulted. The Pandavas were sent into twelve years of forest exile plus a year in hiding. In the forest, sages told them stories, among them Savitri's: knowing her husband Satyavan was fated to die within a year, she married him anyway, and when Yama, the god of death, came for his soul, she followed so faithfully that Yama restored him. Another time, a voice at a lake struck the four younger brothers dead for drinking before answering its questions. Yudhishthira answered them all. Asked the greatest wonder in the world, he said it was that people watch others die every day, yet never believe they themselves will. The voice was Dharma himself, testing him, and the brothers rose again.

When Duryodhana refused them even five villages, war came at Kurukshetra. Krishna would not fight but drove Arjuna's chariot, and gave him the Gita, which Swamiji calls the loftiest of all teachings: work hard, love deeply, but never cling. After eighteen days, Duryodhana fell and the Pandavas won, at a terrible cost.

Years later the brothers and Draupadi set out to walk to heaven through the Himalayas. One by one they fell, until only Yudhishthira and a faithful dog remained. When Indra's chariot came for him, he refused to enter without the dog, even trading away his own merit for it. The dog then revealed himself as Dharma. Yudhishthira's compassion had won him heaven, where he met his brothers again.
For Swamiji, these two epics are encyclopaedias of an ideal life that humanity still has to grow into.
learn: Yudhishthira stood by honesty and loyalty even when it cost him everything, and Savitri refused to give up on the one she loved. Real strength is staying true to your values when shortcuts are on offer.
